title: The earth shook (Matthew 27:27–56)
hook: when someone dies the world keeps going; in Matthew, the world stops
carry: truly this was the son of god
tomorrow: the body needs a grave by nightfall. who steps forward?

segments.voice: A warning from a dream, and water that couldn't wash anything away: have nothing to do with him. Today is hard to hear; if children are listening, you may want to be close.

When someone dies, it can feel wrong that the world keeps going: traffic, notifications, somebody laughing in the next room, a delivery at the door, as if nothing happened. In Matthew, at this death, the world does stop. "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour." Then the veil of the Temple is torn, the earth quakes, rocks split. And a Roman officer at the cross, a centurion, is the one who says it: "Truly this was the Son of God."
screen: `THE WORLD KEEPS GOING.` → `DARKNESS OVER ALL THE LAND.` → `TRULY THIS WAS THE SON OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Matthew tells the hours before plainly. Soldiers put a scarlet robe on Jesus and a crown of thorns, kneel in mockery, then strike him. A man of Cyrene named Simon is made to carry the cross. At Golgotha, a place of a skull, passersby say, "He saved others; himself he cannot save." At the ninth hour Jesus cries with a loud voice, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those are the opening words of Psalm 22, a psalm that begins forsaken and still says my God. He cries again, and yields up the ghost. Then: "the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake." The centurion and those with him, the very men keeping watch over Jesus, see the earthquake, fear greatly, and say the line. And at a distance, still watching: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee's children. So what does this give someone in a week with a loss in it? Two things. Words for the worst moment, borrowed from a psalm: a why that is still addressed to my God. And the women: they couldn't stop anything, and they didn't leave.
screen: `A SCARLET ROBE; SIMON CARRIES THE CROSS.` · `MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY?` · `THE VEIL RENT IN TWAIN.` · `THE WOMEN, STILL WATCHING.` · then, large: `TRULY THIS WAS THE SON OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Choose a moment this afternoon, around the hour Matthew calls the ninth, which some readers count as about three o'clock, and fix it in mind now. Then bring to mind someone grieving this week. If you pray, you can hold them before God with the psalm's first words; if not, just keep them company in your thoughts, the way the women stayed.
The earth shook. Darkness, a torn veil, a quaking earth, and a soldier's words at the cross.
Keep this: truly this was the son of god, said by a centurion who came to guard a cross. Go gently today.

howItsDone: Some churches read the crucifixion on Good Friday, and some Christians keep a time of quiet or prayer in the afternoon, at the hour Matthew calls the ninth.

chat.meaning: At the cross the women couldn't change anything, and they stayed, beholding afar off. Presence can keep a respectful distance.

notes: Hard scene: the review carries a gentle line for parents ('if children are listening, you may want to be close'); the mocking and crucifixion are told plainly and briefly, without graphic detail.

The mocking is told from the soldiers and 'passersby' (27:27–31, 39–40); 27:42 is quoted without naming who said it (in Matthew, the chief priests, scribes and elders). Confirm the framing is careful and fair.
Practice: 'some readers count the ninth hour as about three o'clock' is hedged on purpose (outline practice: pray at three o'clock); confirm.
Graves opened and saints raised (27:52–53) are left out for time.
'A psalm that begins forsaken and still says my God' and the trapdoor's 'turns to praise' rest on Psalm 22:1 and 22:22; confirm.
